title: AI gets more diagnoses right than generalist doctors in medical challenge
content:
AI gets more diagnoses right than generalist doctors in medical challenge
Paul Arnold
Author
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
One of the many challenging parts of being a doctor is diagnosing exactly what is wrong with a patient. This is because numerous illnesses often have overlapping symptoms, which can make the diagnostic journey a long one.
In addition to asking patients questions, doctors may need to order tests and consult medical references or even other professionals. Obviously, for the individual patient, the sooner a diagnosis is reached, the sooner they can start receiving the most appropriate treatment.
Now, in yet another breakthrough for AI, Microsoft researchers claim they have developed a tool that can outperform individual generalist physicians in diagnosing complex medical cases.
It is called DxO, which stands for Diagnostic Orchestrator, and simulates a panel of clinical experts who collaborate to reach a diagnosis.
The diagnostic challenge
To see how well DxO performs and how it compares with medical professionals, researchers developed a testing framework called SDBench, which was essentially an interactive quiz.
The team took 304 published diagnostic cases from the New England Journal of Medicine and 325 emergency department admission records. They turned each of these patient files into a step-by-step test.
At the start of each test, a doctor or DxO was given a summary called a clinical vignette. This included basic details like the patient's age and sex and their main symptoms.
For example, one case started with: "A 29-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital because of sore throat and peritonsillar swelling and bleeding. Symptoms did not abate with antimicrobial therapy."
An AI system acted as a gatekeeper, providing information from the original case file in response to questions and test requests. Once a doctor or DxO felt they had enough information, they submitted a final diagnosis. An AI judge graded the diagnosis against the one recorded in the original case file.
The results are in
The difference between AI and real doctors was striking, as the team reports in a paper published in the journal Science.
Regarding the complex published cases, DxO made an accurate diagnosis 83.2% of the time and achieved 80.3% accuracy on emergency department admission cases. Human doctors, on the other hand, averaged 36.1% and 46.8%, respectively.
There were also clear differences in approach. DxO asked more questions about the patient's background upfront before ordering tests, which could help reduce testing costs.
While AI appears to have come out on top, the researchers state that it doesn't mean it is better than doctors in real-world practice. "These comparisons do not establish superiority over specialists, multidisciplinary teams, or real-world clinical practice."
Additionally, the Microsoft team did not conduct the testing in everyday health care settings. "As a result, SDBench measures diagnostic reasoning under idealized information conditions rather than bedside performance or patient outcomes."
The study authors say future work should explore how doctors and AI systems could work together. They also suggest the technology could be used in medical education and training.

report.summary: Microsoft's DxO AI diagnostic orchestrator outperformed individual generalist doctors on complex published and emergency cases in a new Science study.
report.background: Diagnostic errors are a persistent safety and cost problem: overlapping symptoms, fragmented records and test-heavy workflows can delay correct treatment. AI has already spread through imaging, triage and documentation, but complex diagnostic reasoning—deciding what to ask, which test to order and when to commit—has been harder to benchmark. Microsoft's DxO arrives amid a wave of medical language-model research and heightened scrutiny over hallucination, bias and clinician trust. By adapting published NEJM clinicopathological cases and emergency admissions into interactive quizzes, the study tries to measure sequential reasoning rather than one-shot question answering. The headline comparison is with individual generalist physicians under idealized information conditions, not with specialists or real bedside care, so it is best read as a signal about AI's growing diagnostic orchestration skills and a prompt for rigorous human-AI evaluation.
key_points: DxO, or Diagnostic Orchestrator, is designed as a panel of simulated clinical experts that collaborate. It receives a short clinical vignette, then asks the gatekeeper AI for history, records and test results before submitting a diagnosis—mimicking a structured diagnostic workup rather than a single prompt-response.

Researchers built SDBench from 304 published NEJM diagnostic cases and 325 emergency department admissions. Each case became an interactive quiz with an AI gatekeeper releasing information only when asked; an AI judge scored the final diagnosis against the original record.

DxO diagnosed 83.2% of published complex cases and 80.3% of emergency cases correctly. Individual human generalist doctors averaged 36.1% and 46.8%, respectively—a large gap, though the setup favored exhaustive, low-cost questioning and idealized information.

The AI asked more background and history questions before ordering tests. That pattern could reduce unnecessary testing and costs, but it may also reflect benchmark incentives; real-world medicine involves time pressure, incomplete data, physical exams and accountability.

The authors caution against claiming superiority: DxO was not compared with specialists or multidisciplinary teams, and SDBench measures reasoning under idealized conditions, not bedside outcomes. They call for research on human-AI collaboration and use in medical education.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the study strengthens the case for interactive, sequential medical agents and benchmarks that test information gathering, not just final answers. Developers should expect more emphasis on tool use, uncertainty, audit trails and human oversight, because diagnostic errors carry regulatory and safety consequences. For clinicians, DxO-style systems are more plausible as triage, second-opinion or training aids than replacements; the low doctor scores in an artificial quiz also show how benchmark design shapes conclusions. For patients, near-term benefits may come from faster workups and fewer unnecessary tests, but deployment must wait for prospective trials, bias testing and clear liability rules. The biggest lesson is evaluation: AI claims in medicine need realistic settings and comparison with specialists and care teams.
report.tools: Watch Microsoft Research's DxO and SDBench publications; the paper is in Science (DOI: 10.1126/science.aeh7930). No open-source release is described, so follow the authors' code/data plans. For hands-on exploration, open-source medical LLMs such as Meditron, BioMistral and OpenBioLLM, plus agent frameworks like MedAgents, offer starting points. Pair them with clinical reasoning benchmarks and strong guardrails; do not use them for real diagnosis without validation.
